utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, September 30th, 2009, and I greet Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I also greet Mr. Coric, who is not with us for the moment. Let me also greet the Defence counsels, the eminent members of the OTP, Mr. Kruger and Mr. Stringer, as well as their case manager. And I also greet everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar. He has two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Praljak Defence has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to documents tendered through Witness Slobodan Praljak. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1062. And the Prosecution has submitted its objections to the list of documents tendered for admission by 4D through Witness Zvonimir Skender. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1063. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I have two oral decisions to render, and of course I also greet our witness, because I'd forgotten to welcome him. First oral decision on the motion to tender evidence through Witness Alojz Arbutina. The Praljak Defence filed a motion for the admission of evidence placed on list IC1050 through Witness Alojz Arbutina, who testified on September 22nd, 2009, according to Rule 92 ter. The Trial Chamber notes that neither the Prosecution nor any Defence team -- any other Defence team filed any motion to tender evidence through this witness and that no objection was raised against the Praljak motion. The Trial Chamber thus decides to admit Exhibit 3D03699, tendered through the IC list, on the grounds that it seems to have sufficient probative value, relevance, and reliability, since it is the written statement of Rule 92 ter Witness Alojz Arbutina, statement. Second oral decision. This decision relates to the motion filed by the Praljak Defence to be granted leave to file a response. On 23rd of September, 2009, the Praljak Defence has filed a request with a view to seeking leave to respond. A preliminary response was filed by the Prosecution on the Praljak Defence's request to have written statements tendered into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Praljak Defence would like to file its response within 7 days as of the 28th of October, 2009, onwards. In its decision of the 22nd of September, 2009, the Trial Chamber granted all the parties an extension of time until the 29th of October, 2009, to reply to the request on admission filed by the Praljak Defence on the 14th of September, 2009. The Trial Chamber recalls that the responses are only permitted insofar as the moving party specifies and states that the circumstances are sufficiently compelling and exceptional for the Trial Chamber to grant this request. Consequently, the Trial Chamber holds that the Trial Chamber, as well as the Praljak Defence, must have been made aware of all the potential responses filed by the parties at the request of the Praljak Defence of the 14th of September, 2009, to assess whether or not a response is needed. Therefore, the request to reply to the Praljak motion is premature at this stage. The Trial Chamber asks the Praljak Defence to seize the Trial Chamber of a single motion to seek leave to file a consolidated response to all potential responses by the 29th of October, 2009. In addition, with a view to upholding judicial economy, the Trial Chamber invites the Prosecution to file a single consolidated response in which it will include all the arguments submitted in its preliminary response. The Trial Chamber and all the other parties will only consider this second consolidated reply filed by the Prosecution. This oral decision is a very long decision, but, in short, the Prosecution is being asked to file a single consolidated response, and after that the Praljak Defence, if it deems it is necessary, will file a motion with a view to being granted permission to reply, and the Trial Chamber will rule on the matter with all the elements at hand. The initial request to be granted leave to reply is, as it stands, dismissed. Mr. Kovacic, have you understood me well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your decision. We have fully understood it, and I'm sure you understand why we had to file this motion at this early stage. So now this decision covers it. However, I feel -- and just if we look at page 3, line 18, there seems to be a mistake in the translation there. It's only in the last portion that you mention that you summarise the decision, and that makes it clear now. But from the previous paragraph, it follows, and I'll read it: [In English] "The Trial Chamber asks the Praljak Defence to seize the Trial Chamber of a single motion to seek to file a consolidated response to all potential responses by the 29 October." This is obviously some mistake, because we cannot do it on that day because other parties has -- but from the last paragraph, where you summarise everything, I think it is now clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall read this part again. The mistake stems from the fact that the interpreters did not have the document in question, the decision, which explains why there might be a mistake. Let me read this out slowly. The Trial Chamber invites the Praljak Defence to seize the Chamber of a single request to be permitted to file a consolidated response to all potential responses after the 28th of October, 2009, after the 28th of October, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There are no more dilemmas. Everything is crystal clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, I'd like to greet you once again. I haven't heard you for a long time, and I was beginning to miss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm very delighted to hear that, Your Honour, and of course it's reciprocated. And, Your Honour, wherever I sit in the courtroom, I always seem to be a disembodied pillar, as far as Judge Prandler is concerned. My apologies to Judge Prandler for that, but I know he's there. Your Honour, I have a very brief application on behalf of the Stojic, Praljak and Petkovic Defences. Your Honours gave us leave to put in a reply in relation to a motion which we'd filed for further disclosure under Rule 68. Your Honour, it's ready to file, but it's at around approaching 1800 words. Your Honour knows -- Your Honours know that the word limit is 1500. It's not, I believe, in the discursive style at the moment, Your Honour, so I do ask for an extension by 300 words, and then we are, for practical purposes, ready to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Could we be heard on this, because it was quite a lengthy motion that was filed initially, and if I recall correctly, the Trial Chamber granted all of the Defence teams leave to file an initial motion that exceeded by several hundred the word limit, and now we're going over by several hundred more words again on the reply. So there's a lot of information and a lot of content that appears to be coming in, much more so that's envisioned under the Rules. Once we see this, and I'm not going to take a position on whether the Trial Chamber should grant the requested extension or not, but it may be that based on the very large volume of information that's come in, the Prosecution might request to file some sort of a surrebuttal to this, because, really, it's something that is now quite excessive, in terms of the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just call it -- briefly, I don't want to get into a big squabble, I appreciate Mr. Stringer's position. Your Honour, he -- no doubt, he can reserve his position on this. We just make the point that the number of words is really a separate issue from whether it is genuinely a reply, and so far as the points in the reply are genuinely a matter of reply, then there wouldn't be any real room for any further filing in relation to this matter. But, Your Honour, it's pointless. Like Mr. Stringer, I'd say let's then see what happens and see what application he might make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, grants the request filed by Mr. Stewart and accords you 180 words -- 1.800 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.800 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I understood. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I'd like to greet you once again. Let me remind you that you have 16 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm going to try, within my time-limit, to complete my cross-examination, but I might need a little more time to finish this document, and I agree to that time being deducted from the time allotted to me. And I wanted to ask the usher, yes, for his help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but with respect to what my colleague Ms. Nozica just said, so that it goes down in the record, I'd like to present the Petkovic Defence's position. Since during the Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic, for an additional second of examination of the witness, we needed to file a special request and explain the reasons for which we were requesting additional time. I'd just like it to go down on the record that any other decision and any other rules during the Petkovic -- during the Petkovic Defence we will consider to be an upset in the equality of rights at this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, can you tell us why you need some extra time? Could you detail this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can explain in greater detail, but I'd like to ask the usher to provide the new binder of documents to the Court. I just need the additional time because of an answer given by the witness yesterday, the answers related to mobilisation in Gornji Vakuf, in actual fact. There are documents which speak differently to the answer given by the witness yesterday, so I have prepared documents which speak of the existence of an administration and office in Gornji Vakuf. And yesterday's answers by this witness were the reason why I requested additional time. I will do my very best to make use of the 16 minutes I have at my disposal wisely, but I'd just like to mention that regardless of the position taken by the Petkovic Defence team - I cannot object, everybody has the right to raise an objection - but I think that with all the witnesses so far in the Praljak Defence, the Praljak Defence, including the Petkovic Defence, did receive additional time if they needed it from the overall time they were allotted. Now, if we're going to change the rules again, I am going to adhere to that, and every time I'm going to explain in great detail why I need extra time. I'm doing this today because yesterday the answers given by the witness gave rise to the necessity for an additional five minutes of examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have understood. At least I have understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, unfortunately, during my studies I did not pay full attention to accounting, but you probably will be in a state of telling us how much your reserve is in time. How much time allotted to you have you not yet exhausted?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think at least seven hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. That's the issue. You will not get additional time. No one got any so far. And that's fine, then. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, I showed you a document yesterday. It was 4D308, and it's in that larger binder that we were dealing with yesterday. 4D308 is the number, and I said yesterday that it was also 3D796. Therefore, it has two numbers, and it was under the latter number that it was made an exhibit. It's a report from a meeting of commanders from the Military District of North-West Herzegovina of the 26th of October, 2003. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed it yesterday. Anyway, in point 2, mobilisation is discussed, and in point 4, deserters are mentioned. Now, Mr. Tokic, from this text, and you can read through it, it says to deal with the status of deserters and, in that connection, elaborate uniform criteria which will be applied to all military conscripts who fled or who are still avoiding their responsibilities in the homeland war. Now, Mr. Tokic, from this text, we can conclude that those participating in the meeting, you among them, considered deserters to be military conscripts who failed to respond to the mobilisation call-up. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, allow me to say good morning to Their Honours and everybody else in the courtroom first. But you're not right, it does not refer to military conscripts who were not mobilised. It refers to those military conscripts who were members of units and later on left the area of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's an error in the transcript, but I was told that I said it was document 4D308, whereas it is document 3D803. So I got that wrong. Thank you. Now, you know what I don't understand here? It's this -- 803 is the number, 4D803. That's right. Now, in point 4, it says: "Military conscripts who are still avoiding to comply with their responsibilities." That is why I thought you referred to the latter. Now, Mr. Tokic, tell me, please, following a request from the brigade, the Administration for Mobilisation mobilises a soldier and sends him to a unit, and he is given a military ID and becomes a full-fledged member of the brigade. If, after that, that person deserts, isn't it the brigade command which is supposed to take the necessary steps to take him into custody through the brigade military police, and if they fail to do so, then that they should file a criminal report against him? Wasn't that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, from my conduct as a commander, and you see that there were 279 persons who -- against whom criminal reports were filed, now, the problem that a commander has when he's in the field is when he contacts the military police or the security service of the military police, the military conscript already at that time is not in the area of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, he is inaccessible, they can't reach him. And for us, who were soldiers, regardless of our assignments and posts, that was a difficult situation, and that is why we asked that the authorities of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna should take steps to prevent people being able to escape through a border that was as hollow as a Swiss cheese.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted us to clear that up. That is to say, it was the command of the unit that decides on these matters. You've just explained that. Can we now take a look at document P6017 again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, please, if you will allow me, we will continue looking at document 4D803. I would like you to look at paragraph 11, please. Registrar, could you show us paragraph 11, please, because for the time being we can only see paragraph 6 in English, paragraph 8 in B/C/S. So we've got paragraph 11 in English. I'd like to see paragraph 11 in B/C/S as well, please. In your language, you can see paragraph 11 now. This meeting which was held, which you attended, since your name is mentioned here, as well as Siljeg's, Glasnovic, Suskar [phoen], Sikic [phoen], Tokic, you, Pavlovic, Djeric, and two other people, you are asking for the Government of the Republic of Croatia to hand out no more refugee cards to the conscripts who have left the municipalities in Herceg-Bosna. They could then return to the brigades. You are saying that it is important for the Croatian government to stop handing out refugee cards. When I saw this mentioned in the text, I set this against the backdrop of a notion which you are familiar with and which the lawyers and the Prosecution have in mind; that is, that of the JCE, the joint criminal enterprise. What I would like to know from you, Witness, is this: Is it logical in any way that the Croatian government let's the Croatian deserters come in, give them refugee cards, when, on the other hand, the Croatian government is helping the Community of Herceg-Bosna by providing them with soldiers? Does this make sense to you? If you don't understand my question, I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Your Honour, could you rephrase that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me rephrase my question. We have a situation in which the soldiers, the conscripts, are deserting and go to the Republic of Croatia. In the Republic of Croatia, they're handed out refugee cards. In other words, they don't come back again. And in addition, we are being told that the Republic of Croatia is helping the forces of Herceg-Bosna directly. I would like to know from you whether there is not a contradiction here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we discuss the situation as commanders, we address the government first of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, with the task of undertaking the necessary measures. We ask them to take the necessary measures so that the out-flow of military conscripts from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were soldiers in the units of the Croatian Defence Council, should be stopped. At the same time, we asked them to act as mediators to see that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, when they see these people coming in without the necessary papers and procedure, does not provide them and accord them refugee status. That is what soldiers can do and must do so as to retain the number of conscripts necessary for the units, which guarantees that they will be able to fulfill their tasks as a unit. Now, when it comes to the second half of your question, what I can say is this: I don't know that the Republic of Croatia helped us by sending their soldiers to us in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know that they offered that assistance. So you asked me to conclude whether it's contradictory. I really can't say. I know what I signed and subscribed to, as a commander, and who I contacted in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The second question now. When you were fighting, since you were a commander, at some point did you have the feeling or the proof that the Croatian government out of Zagreb was controlling your military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, let us look again at document P6017. This is the data breakdown per municipalities, and I'm going to ask you to look at this portion that refers to Uskoplje municipality. That's page 3 in Croatian and page 5 in English. It says here, Mr. Tokic, that Uskoplje municipality had 10.700 inhabitants, that there were 1.020 military conscripts in operative units, there were 273 of them in home guards, and it also said that 256 criminal reports had been filed. Yesterday, in response to my question whether you can confirm this data, you said yesterday that you were not sure whether these figures are correct. Mr. Tokic, in your statement given to Mr. Praljak's Defence in 2005, November 2005, you said something different about this subject, and that was the underlying reason for all my questions relating to mobilisation. So, therefore, let us look at this portion from your statement, which is document 3D3712. It's a new binder that I've given you today. It's on page 28, and I'm going to read only this specific portion, page 28, the very top of it, and I'm talking about the Croatian version, and in the English it's page 26. I'm going to read only this particular portion: "At one point, the mobilisation rate of this unit was 18.6 per cent. We, in the army, say that the standard mobilisation rate is 10 per cent. If you apply this to 10.700 Croats, according to the census, 10 per cent is 1.070, and our unit had 1300 men, a brigade, plus military police, plus MUP, plus the battalion of Bruno Busic." So in total around 1600. Mr. Tokic, as we can see from this statement of yours, all this information stated in the document presented by me to you, which is document P6017, are identical. It says here that there was a total of 10.709 inhabitants, and the total of operational units and home guard units makes 1300 men. That was actually the reason why I asked you yesterday whether, in your municipality and your brigades, the mobilisation was successful. That was, by the way, my conclusion. Let me first ask you this: Did you prepare and did you make this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you stand behind this particular paragraph? I'm insisting on that.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All the figures that you provided in 2005, in November, are almost identical to those given in document P6017?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify this. When we were conducting mobilisation, there was no Defence office of Uskoplje. The mobilisation was carried out by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, we'll come to the office. What I am focused here on --

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was the situation at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters, but I had to intervene. I only asked you about this particular portion which I found somewhat confusing when you said that you were not sure about the veracity of this information. On the other hand, I found identical information in your statement. As to when the office was set up and how it started working is a different matter. My question was whether the information provided by you, in your statement, is almost identical to the information contained in the document that I showed to you. One could have gained an impression that I'm showing you something that was incorrect or something that you were not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam counsel, if I may answer and provide clarification. I was one of those who took part in the meeting of the North-West Operation Zone. My views are known. However, certain municipalities had more serious problems than my municipality. I described the situation in my municipality, and I said that I was dissatisfied how those who left the units of their own volition were treated and who were not accessible to my military police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly the clarification that I needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm really ashamed that I have to say this again and again and again, but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the interpretation asked you and, of course, the witness to slow down, number 1, and then to hold a pause between the question and the answer, as number 2. Please kindly follow this. I know that you are pressed by time pressure, but, anyway, please try to comply with this request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to the Chamber. You can only imagine, honourable Judge, how shameful it is for me to be reminded by you so many times, but this is a problem that stems from the fact that we speak the same language. It goes well when we have slow speak, but when it comes to some clarifications, it creates problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, another question concerning mobilisation. You said that you were not aware of the existence of the Defence office in Uskoplje. They were established there and they were in charge of conducting mobilisation. I'm going to show you a number of documents who are also in this new binder, and we shall see whether you remember whether this office really existed. For that purpose, could you please look at document P700. That's a proposal made by Mr. Bruno Stojic to adopt a decision on the number and the seats of Defence offices. On the other side -- on the other page, you see the Tomislavgrad Administration, and under 8, within Tomislavgrad Administration, you can see which area it covers. This decision was taken on the 18th November 1992, at the meeting of the HVO HZ-HB, and that's P700. Let us just look now at the final document, which is P767, so that's the minutes of the HVO meeting, 767. And please look at document 2D3055. Have you found it? You can find it in this additional binder that you received, and it's the last document. You did. Thank you. Here, Mr. Brano Matijanic has been appointed by Mr. Stojic, the chief of the Office for Defence in Gornji Vakuf. Were you familiar with this gentleman and did you know that he was working at this office? I would just like to refresh your memory about this issue.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He had an office in Pidris.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was the Defence office of Uskoplje municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with one member of staff only.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. But, nevertheless, a Defence office?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you can see and judge for yourself whether one person could have done the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, in the statement of yours that I read out to you, this job was done very satisfactorily, because a high percentage of citizens were mobilised to your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell this to you for the second time. Mobilisation was carried out by the Municipal Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But the Defence office was part of that staff?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay, let's move to another topic. Can we now go back to document 4D803. I would just like to address two items from this document. And the next one we're going to look at is item 7. You say here: "Create a single disciplinary book to comply with the conditions --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, if I understand correctly, you are no longer talking about mobilisation. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I have only two topics to ask this witness about regarding this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But do these questions still address mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not about mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, I have a follow-up question regarding mobilisation. I know that you are a professor and that you teach defence matters, so you obviously seem to be a specialist in this area. In the interview you gave, you explained that there were 1.070 Croats, and with a 10 per cent mobilisation you should end up with about 1.000, but altogether you ended up being 1.600, whereas the others in the TO were 2.100, and you seem to be fairly satisfied with the situation. However, when I look at all this and when I note that during war you can only mobilise 10 per cent of the troops, I can only draw from this that there must be a huge problem. If I compare this with other conflicts, for example, modern conflicts like World War I, mobilisation was almost 100 per cent of troops, at least in some countries, but here, in your conflict, you only ended up with 10 per cent. I can only draw from this that there must have been reasons for this. So is it that these so-called conscripts who deserted just deserted because they thought it wasn't their war, they didn't want to wage this -- they didn't want to fight for this cause, or was it because there was no state and that they didn't feel that they were soldiers of a specific state; that they felt that if they were conscripted, they were more like private militiamen and it was not their war? Were they afraid of the Serbs, maybe, because the Serbs were a daunting force and they thought that the war was lost before even being waged? These are all reasons I'm giving you. You know, there might be others, but can you tell us how you can explain that you only ended up with this 10 per cent ratio, when it came to mobilisation, that only 10 per cent of the men actually volunteered and that the others were very hard to mobilise? Were there any far-reaching reasons behind this, and if so, could you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, speaking about mobilisation, I was familiar with some of the aspects of this particular area. I'm not saying that I'm an expert, but the fact is, quite simply, that in the area of Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje municipalities, of the 10.700 potential military conscripts, about 18 per cent of them were mobilised. What we tried to do was to make maximum effort, because a number of our soldiers were out of actions as a result of military operations that we had had, a number of soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's no problem. What I would like to tell you, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, with all due respect, that your information about 100 per cent success mobilisation is wrong. There is no single war that one can achieve that high percentage of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. I note this down. Could you please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, speaking about the efforts that we were making in the municipality where I was the commander, it proved to be satisfactory, at least in theoretical terms. The problem was with the additional reinforcements, and this is where the Defence office comes into play. When a unit asks for additional manpower, according to the assignment, then the Defence office should provide new conscripts, provided they have them ready on the field, but with that you have to take into account a supposition that they might flee, because we say only fools are not afraid of death and war. Some people managed to control their fear better, some didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there was a mistake. So not to elaborate further, perhaps you could ask the witness was the interpretation wrong or did I hear wrong, but at the beginning, in response to your question, on page 20, line 24, he said that in Uskoplje, out of 10.700 potential military conscripts, about 18 per cent. So obviously this figure, 10.700, refers to the number of inhabitants, the population. So there's some short-circuit there, some misunderstanding, because the mistakes can multiply if we let that go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, when you said that there were 10.700 potential soldiers, you know, when I made reference to countries where mobilisation was at 100 per cent, it was only potential soldiers. Of course, you're not going to mobilise the sick, the mad-men, those who are in hospital, and so forth. So when I talk about the potential soldiers, those who are able-bodied -- so when you talked about 10.700 potential conscripts, were you referring to the population, as a whole, or only to the able-bodied men who could have borne a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was referring to the overall population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're talking about the entire population. Very well. Ms. Nozica, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd just like to confirm something. I was going to do this at the end, but I'd like to do it now. In document 3D3712 - it is a statement, the statement by Mr. Tokic, in fact - and in document P6017, is it right that the number there is 10.700 Croats, it says, so the overall population? There was no mention of the number of potential military conscripts, just to make that point clear. Now, Mr. Tokic, I asked you something related to point 7 of document 803, and that is it reads: "Make universal disciplinary book for the units ..." Now, you know that there was a book of rules on discipline in the HZ-HB HVO; you knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So can we look at the document? It is P293 in your binder. I think it's the next document in line. And in those rules on discipline adopted by Mr. Mate Boban, president of the HZ-HB, from Article 101 we have the wartime situation. Now, can you remember why, at the meeting, this conclusion was made whereby a uniform rules of military discipline should be passed? Because we see that this is one, one it says that should be in line with wartime conditions. Now, were there any comments made about that at the meeting or why this observation was made, if you can remember? If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but, in principle, these -- these rules on military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, did you listen when Judge Prandler spoke? He said, Wait until the question is translated. You have shot along long before that. Please start your answer again, and please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will bear that in mind, and I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you whether you could remember why this conclusion on the rules governing military discipline were passed at this meeting and adopted at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the units, quite simply, did not receive any book of rules in the field, so we couldn't apply it if we didn't have it in the first place in sufficient copies and distributed to those to whom it referred, and the role to implement rules goes from company commanders onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this meeting, Mr. Tokic, was held on the 26th of October, 1993, and you now say that the commanders didn't have this set of rules. Did you apply the rules, yourself, while you were commander, even before this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there were several guide-lines and instructions, and we applied them, but this book of rules just consolidated all those guide-lines and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This was passed on the 3rd of July, 1992, Witness. It could not consolidate anything. It was a basic act and was passed and adopted on the 3rd of July, 1992. But let's move on to the next document, which is 5D2022, and that's a letter signed by the deputy commander of the military district, Mr. Ante Govorusic, and he refers to an order there from the commander of the Main Staff, dated the 17th of September, 1993, with respect to implementing the disciplinary measures taken, and here against a member of the armed forces of the HZ-HB on the basis of the rules governing military discipline and the mistakes made, and that these measures of custody will be enforced if Dretelj prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down. It is not possible to interpret at this rate. Thank you. And a reference to where the counsel is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The number of the document is right, 5D5022.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So on the 23rd of September, 10 days before this meeting, each and every commander in the field received this order, which speaks of the way and where the perpetrators of misdemeanors and crimes will serve their sentence. Do you agree with me that at least at that time all the commanders knew about this and that there was a set of rules, and they knew how those rules should be implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the -- if the other commanders knew about this, but I received this order, myself, and I applied these rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask, in closing, to broach just one topic referring to the meeting. It is 4D803, the document I'd like to refer to once again, 4D803, the conclusions from your meeting. And we're going to take a look at conclusion number 13 there, the last line. It says: "To determine authorisation and manner in which appointments are to be proposed, and the establishment of SIS, itself." Now, Mr. Tokic, you, as a commander, did you know in what way the officers of SIS in your brigade are proposed and appointed?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know the manner in which this was done, what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about you, yourself, Mr. Tokic? Did you propose any members for SIS from your brigade? Did you put them forward, did you take part in the selection process?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Could you give me some names of the SIS person? In the case of Zvonko Katovic, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber in what way you did this? In what way did you go about it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked our opinion. The commander of the unit was asked his opinion about somebody, whether they had the necessary qualifications for the job and other necessary knowledge for them to be -- become a member of the Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who asked for this information?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Security Service that required that information, itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While you were the commander, did you ever receive a decision to appoint somebody, Mr. Katovic, or anybody else, for that matter? Did you see the process of somebody being appointed and a document to that effect? But just wait for me to finish and then you can continue with your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a decision on paper for Mr. Josip Sen [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who signed that decision?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whose signature was on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, what institution, then?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institution was the Security Service from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. The Administration for Security, in actual fact. That's what it was called, I think. Thank you. Now, I've prepared two more documents. I'll show the first one, which is 2D567. It is a decision on the internal establishment of the Defence Department, and you need not have been fully informed about that, but it, too, speaks of the manner in which people were elected and forces, and it says the assistant commanders of the brigades for security are appointed by the head of the Defence Department. That is to be found in item 4, at the proposal of the assistant head for security. And it says for all other operatives and officials in the Sector for Security, it is the assistant head for security who disposes of them, along with previous agreement from the representative of the Defence Department or an individual whom he authorises. Now, since you said that you received a decision of that kind on paper, it was probably a decision signed by the head of the department, the administration, so you knew how this worked in practice. Now we have the next decision, which is slightly amended, but we won't go into that. And now linked to the situation of how people proposed individuals from the ground, from the field, the last document we'll look at is 2D3053. It's a report dated the 5th of November, 1993, and it is signed precisely by Mr. Katovic, as you told us. It is sent by GSRHB, Ivan Lucic, or, rather, the Main Staff of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna personally to Ivan Lucic, and it says here that the SIS in the brigade does not have a single heavy-duty vehicle, or any other vehicle, and it was difficult to inspect the defence lines, but they did their best to tour the defence lines and talk to the soldiers there. This was done by members of SIS in their part of the terrain, and it says the touring of the terrain was carried out by the brigade commander, he inspected the terrain. Now, what I'm interested here is whether the situation was as it is described here, that you had a shortage of vehicles and everything else, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the unit plans its tasks and assignments, and if it can do -- carry out a number of them with just one vehicle, then it does so, and the vehicle is provided by the Logistics Department. There's usually one vehicle, and everybody else, if they need more, have to apply for more vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. So the answer is that this situation was correctly described here. Now, going on to the next paragraph, it says: "I, as head of SIS in the brigade, was taken up with negotiations with the Muslim side, discussing the exchange of bodies and soldiers killed." And then the next paragraph goes on to say with the departure of Ivica Crnov to the brigade's 1st Battalion, there was no SIS member for a month because nobody wanted to take up that duty, and those who did want to were not suitable -- were not found suitable by the brigade commander, Zrinko Tokic, or the president of the HVO, Ivan Saric. Now, Mr. Tokic, is that what you were telling us? Is that what you were saying, that you were asked to provide your opinion as to whether somebody was suitable or not?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we were asked for our opinion. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, it goes on to say that the SIS clerk in the brigade, Zdravko Alvir, was late on his return from a private trip to Zagreb, so the brigade commander ordered that he be reassigned to the infantry, and nobody replaced him, so that this made the work of the service impossible. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an -- is a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mean the last sentence is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's move on to page 2 of that same document. Do you remember -- it says: "I, as chief of SIS in the brigade, have been asked to move to the Rama SIS Centre, and although I received an oral approval from the brigade commander and the president of the HVO, both oral and written approvals, I still have not taken up my duties there because the two aforementioned men cannot agree who to choose to become the SIS chief in the brigade, and so this makes the work of the service even more difficult." Is that correct, sir? Do you remember? Do you remember that you gave your oral approval?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, when any officer was to be promoted, you would give approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I come to my last question. When your brigade -- when it came to your brigade, then this conclusion wouldn't have been made, right, because obviously you knew the way in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Ms. Nozica's last question, and this will be deducted from her time, anyway, because she ran over her 45-minute allotment, I have a question. On this document, we see that in order to appoint an SIS -- a person for the SIS, the brigade commander had to intervene, as well as the HV [as interpreted] president, the local HV [as interpreted] president, and here it was Mr. Ceric. Now, this is what I would like to know. In exercising your military command, were you constrained by a control coming from the HVO president or were you fully independent and did you only report to the commander of the HVO in the operational zone, or was there some kind of supervision exercised by the political -- municipal political authority of the HV [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a brigade commander in the hierarchy is responsible to the commander of the West Herzegovina Operation Zone. However, within the brigade there are sections that sent out reports along different channels, and I'm talking about the security section and the information and propaganda section. These two operated outside of the remit of the commander, but, however, in order to provide good-quality communication they should have provided information horizontally, that is to say, to the commander as well, but they also were requested to send reports to their superiors as well. So there was a certain kind of supervision imposed on a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you haven't answered my question. My question was an extremely precise question. I'm asking you this: As you exercised your command, I wanted to know if in any way you were controlled, supervised, by the political authority in the municipality. This is an extremely precise question, and you are telling me that in the brigade there were units, there were various channels. You quote Information and Propaganda. If that's the case, you should have told me that this depended on the president of the local HVO. And you are giving us a speech. I'm wanting you to answer my question. My question is extremely precise, and when I put a question, it is because it is an important question. I don't put a question for the sake of putting a question, and I set it against the backdrop of this entire case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, speaking about the appointment of these officers, this was more within the responsibility of the president of the local HVO and all the command duties were in the hands of a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your answer, you say when it came to choosing some of the officers, the local president gave his advice, but as far as exercising the command was concerned, this came under the responsibility of the military authorities? This is exactly what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have finished my cross-examination. Nevertheless, I would like to ask one more question in regard to his last answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The heads of SIS and the IPD, were they within the scope of your command? You said that they provided information. I'm only asking you whether they were part of the command of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were my assistants, and they were part of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to put a question to Mr. Karnavas, but my colleague would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question regarding this same document. At one point, the passage regarding Zdravko Alvir was put to you, a person who returned belatedly and then was ordered to serve in the infantry. The report here says that, therefore, the work Alvir was supposed to do, the clerk work, was not done by someone else, and this hindered the work of SIS. You have simply brushed this away by saying it's a lie. That's not really, in itself, convincing. Could you be more precise? What do you mean, "is a lie"? Is it a lie that Zdravko Alvir was late on his return from a private trip? Is that a lie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me to give you an explanation. Zdravko Alvir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I asked you a very precise question, a yes-or-no question. When you said this is a lie, does this refer to the fact that Zdravko Alvir returned belatedly; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot answer this question with yes or no. You have to allow me to explain why Zdravko Alvir was transferred to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Normally, the rules here are is that someone puts a question and the witness is invited to answer that question. I do not think it is impossible to answer this question. I will go on. It's not the only question, but it seems that your answer is negative. You say it is not a lie that Zdravko Alvir returned late?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Then is it a lie that you ordered him to be reassigned to infantry? And here I allow you to give an explanation, why you did so, if you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Zdravko Alvir was in the brigade staff during combat operations on the line in the town between the post office and MUP and bus depot. Since I had received information that BH Army units were deployed in two positions or, actually, broke through these lines in two places, I asked a security officer to take certain direction in order to survey the situation at the post office feature, and that the focus of defence, I decided as a brigade commander, would be to go on. After having consolidated the defence line, I tried -- started looking for reasons why Zdravko Alvir failed to go into the direction that he had been ordered to go. He said that he didn't dare do that because he had never been in town while shooting was on. After that, I decided that because he was late and he performed poorly on the line, to transfer him to the infantry, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then there is a last limb of this chain of information in the paragraph to be answered. The report says that the fact that Zdravko Alvir was removed from his work for SIS, I quote, "seriously impaired" the work of the service. Is that a lie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the assessment made by this officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you are not saying that the assessment is wrong, or are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying it's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think that has brought some clarity in this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you had 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to use them, Your Honour. I'm going to use them, and this last demonstration by Judge Trechsel sort of gives us a good impression as to why sometimes explanations need to be given after a yes or no or a very brief answer, such as, It's a lie, because it may contain lots of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to just discuss with you very briefly the events in general, because I'm not sure that we really have been able to, at least from your point of view, develop the narrative of the events that were unfolding starting, say, from the spring to -- late spring or early summer of 1992 onwards in that particular area. So if you could take a couple of minutes and please describe to us what was the atmosphere like in that area, because the follow-up question to that is going to be, and I'll just put it to you right now, is: Looking back now on the events, would it have been possible at the time to do things differently to avoid any conflicts between the Muslims and the Croats living in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, if I may start with the conflict which took place in June 1992. After that, we signed an agreement on the 27th of June, 1992, and quite simply pulled out our units from any combat contact. We established communication lines with the command of the BH Army in order to create conditions for them to return to the positions that they had abandoned on Radusa Hill facing the Army of Republika Srpska. We have linked up check-points of military police set up at the entry point to the town from Prozor and Novi Travnik respectively, as well as from the direction of Bugojno. I managed to reassure the army commander that he should as well take out his unit by the end of July to the defence line in the area of Bugojno municipality, facing the Army of Republika Srpska on the positions Humac, Jazvenik, and Skrtsko Brdo. So we did everything possible in order to normalise the situation. On the 15th of August, 1992, when the Army of Republika Srpska launched an attack on our lines in Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, and Bugojno, we acted in concert and repelled this attack. My scouting company, along with the Anti-Sabotage Detachment of the Bugojno Brigade, defended Rusac and managed to stop the Serbian attack on the line facing Crvena Zemlja. However, a situation emerged in which HVO units and the army units clashed in Prozor. This all put us back in the old positions when we were looking at each other with mistrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right here. Why did the clash occur? Because it's important for us to have context. I mean, you have a common enemy, but now two allied forces or peoples are clashing among themselves, so what is happening, why it's happening? Please explain that to us, who were not there and don't know the dynamics at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to know the details of the context in which it happened. In most cases, the situation in the neighbouring municipalities reflected and had its impact on the situation in Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje. We were bound, along the chain of command, to carry out the task given to us by superior commands. Therefore, Mr. Agic asked me to let through an anti-sabotage Detachment commanded by Goran Cizic [phoen] from the staff in Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje and allow it to link up with the 2nd Battalion simply in order to provide defence of Pridvorci and Crni Vrh, or that is how he put it. I had to respond by saying that I couldn't do that and I wouldn't allow that. After that, they put their units on full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right here, because again you indicated that there was some mistrust in your previous answer, and now you're being asked specifically what would appear, at least to some of us, to be a reasonable request, and you respond rather unreasonably at the time. That's the impression that one might get. So if you could explain, why was there this mistrust between the Muslims and the Croats at that time, in that area, and why you, in effect, would deny access which then caused, you know, the ABiH to go on full alert?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the fundamental misunderstanding lies in the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the position of the three peoples living there. And in military terms, because I was performing military duties of a commander, and that is something that I had to do, and it is not normal for a commander to let through his combat lines somebody who can jeopardise or even effectively cause losses to the units of the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, again, let me stop you here. Why would -- I mean, assuming that you're both working in conjunction with each other, coordinating your efforts against a common enemy, why would you then -- why are you saying what you just told us, that you're worried that they may even cause -- or jeopardise or cause losses? I mean, this is something that we need to understand.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of October, you had the conflict in Rama, and that was a conflict in which the BH Army forces and the HVO forces took part. Now, other people taking part in the conflict was the 2nd Battalion, forces from outside of the 317th Brigade, for example, from Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje. The commander assessed that the 2nd Battalion troops weren't sufficient for him to carry out his assignment. Now, I couldn't block the forces of the 2nd Battalion because I -- they were outside the area in which I was organised and my men, so for that reason it is clear that the conflict could flare up and spill over into another municipality, regardless of what I did or Mr. Agic did. So on that day, too, we were in the hotel together with 22 other citizens or intellectuals, if you will, from the Croatian and Bosniak side. We were sitting there and organising a peace march. But it did not bear fruit, and on the 23rd, the shooting started. So that simply is something that the army was not able to resolve on its own. The problem didn't lie with the army. The army was established and set up to take up its positions in that given area and, first of all, to put up an active defence in defending the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje area from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if the army isn't responsible -- we might want to take the break at this point, and I'll pick up from there. And I believe I do have about seven or eight minutes left, Your Honours, but I will pick up from that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have five minutes left, but I think the best is to finish now, before the break, and then we'll have the break once you're done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would have liked to be put back in the picture, as it were. Your initial question, Mr. Karnavas, as I recorded it, was: What was the atmosphere in late spring/summer of -- now we are in October, and I just wonder whether this is in the line you were asking or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is. What I'm trying -- what I wish to do is paint a picture of what is happening throughout -- because there is a continuum, and then we'll get to the point that he is testifying, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- I don't want to give any answers or suggestions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you've indicated that the army wasn't the problem, and, very briefly, because they were told to go there and take up these positions. If the army wasn't the problem, who was the problem, then?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I didn't say that in the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje area the army was the problem. We cooperated on a local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said that it wasn't the problem, that it was not the problem, and I'm asking you: If the army was not the problem, who was, or what caused the problem?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to answer by saying that there were different expectations with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina's establishment and that this was reflected in the field, on the ground, and that it was a problem. It was a problem of how to position the municipality of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think I understand where you're going because I've been in the case for four years, but we need concrete answers. So you're talking -- let's say you're talking to somebody who doesn't know the events. What does that answer mean? Give me, specifically, what is the problem, who is the problem, who's causing the problem? You're saying the expectation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's a dissertation. That's worth 10 hours of discussion. Give me, concretely, what do you think was the problem at that point in time in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Counsel, the problem at the time was this: There was a conflict between the HVO and BH Army in Prozor municipality, and it spilt over into Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje. And taking part in that conflict were units of the 2nd Battalion, the 317th Mountain Brigade, in actual fact, and if we had a map before us, you would be able to see that this is the settlement of Voljevac, Pridvorci, et cetera, and that they were attacking along the axis of Najnik [phoen] and Jurici, together with the units from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. That gets us -- that helps us. Now, we're in October. I only have a couple of minutes. From late October, we go into January. What's happening there? And tell us exactly when is it that the conflict in January begins, because the Prosecution has the theory, we've presented evidence to the contrary, but you can tell us, very briefly, what happens during that short period of time and when the conflict begins in earnest.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict began in January, towards evening on the 11th, in fact, the 11th of January, 1993, a little before 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why did it begin? Because you have October, things calm down, and then from October to January, things pick up again. Why -- what's happening in that area in Gornji Vakuf? And then the last question that goes with that is if you could tell us when the HVO civilian government actually begins to function.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the reasons for the conflict beginning in January, the BH Army brought in 305 members of the Jajce Brigade, and from December onwards they deployed these men along the Gornji Vakuf area. After that, there was the Christmas break and the Christmas holidays, and we decorated the part of town inhabited by the Croats, and the Croats, on their houses, put up the Christmas decorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, some people didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that done specifically to provoke and to initiate a war, because we had a Prosecutor here just only a couple of days ago saying that the Croats were looking for a war and were pursuing a war? Is that the reason, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, finally, we have to take the break. When did the civilian government begin to function in earnest in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think that right up to -- well, Zdravko Batinic, as president of the Municipal Assembly, went on the 11th to take up his duties, so that means that in January the Croats were still in the bodies of power and authority in the Gornji Vakuf municipality, as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about the HVO. When you say that -- when he was -- when Batinic was president of the Municipal Assembly, but that was not -- it had nothing to do with the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council was set up by a decision of the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, but I'm asking you when it began to function as a government, because the impression that you may be leaving is that as of that date, there was a Croatian HVO government in place in Gornji Vakuf, throughout that period, functioning as a government.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Counsel, I said that the Croats were present in the joint bodies of authority in Gornji Vakuf up until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. I want to thank you very, very much for coming here to give your evidence. Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank the interpreters for their extra time and effort.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll break for 20 minutes, and then after the break we will give the floor to Mr. Kruger for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I welcome Mr. Scott, who's with us. Before giving the floor to Mr. Kruger, the Trial Chamber would like to ask Mr. Stringer to confirm that for the last two witnesses of the Praljak Defence, that for his cross-examination he wants two hours for each of these witnesses. Is that it, Mr. Stringer? These are Witnesses Juric and Witness Curcic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President. I apologise if the letter wasn't clear on that. The Prosecution is requesting two hours for each of them, so it would be two hours for Juric and then two hours for Curcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, the Trial Chamber will render its decision. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I would just like to take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that the Petkovic Defence will have a request for additional time to examine Witness Curcic because we consider that he has some very relevant knowledge of benefit to the Trial Chamber and everyone. And if that is important for the planning and scheduling of the courtroom, I wanted to inform you of that. And we assume that 45 minutes, up to an hour, would be the time we needed, that the Petkovic Defence will need. We don't think he is a hostile witness, and we do believe that it would be fair to deduct that time from the overall time allotted to the Petkovic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your request is noted down on the transcript. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, colleagues, everybody else in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, if I could just make certain that the Coric Defence weren't going to use their 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have already said that I'm not going to use those 15 minutes, and I have already stated that if there's no need, then I won't be conducting a cross-examination. And as I see now, I'll stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tokic. Sir, I'd first like to ask you a few general questions about General Praljak. During January 1993, is it correct that General Praljak was referred to in Gornji Vakuf by the name of Brada?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, it's true that General Praljak was called "Brada," among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in January, from your evidence thus far, it's clear that you were aware of the presence of General Praljak in the Gornji Vakuf region or Uskoplje region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You were aware at that stage, I suppose, that General Praljak was not officially a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that he only became commander of the Main Staff in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those details, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You were aware, of course, that in January 1993, General Petkovic was the Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Be that as it may, General Praljak, you did not doubt his authority, in January 1993, to also issue orders and commands to you and your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the commander of the Military District of Tomislavgrad issued orders to me. In this case, that was Mr. Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with General Praljak, personally, during January 1993? I recall that you and he issued a joint command at some stage.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when I went to attend the briefings at the forward command post of the operative zone in Prozor, that is, I would see General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And these briefings that you attended, was that in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes, up until the 13th, while I was able to move around freely along the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, we'll get to those briefings in a moment. From your statement -- I'd just like to refer you to your statement, and it's, in the English version, on page 27. Unfortunately, I didn't check in which part it is in your section, but I will read to you what you stated. And I would just like you to confirm whether this is actually accurate: "He would get to --" talking about General Praljak, this is: "He would get to know how things were at the front. He would survey the terrain, and he would personally go to see the defence facilities, so I don't think that any of the Uskoplje soldiers or commanders could have anything negative to say about communication with the general." Do you agree with that? Is that -- do you stand by what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand fully by what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You also said in your statement - I think it's the same page - you say: "I, being commander of a unit, would have to go to daily briefings, and I had to come either to the forward commanding post of Tomislavgrad gathering place at Dekorativ or to the forward command post here at Pidris. Anyway, during those briefings led by General Praljak, all unit commanders that had been engaged in actions at Uskoplje front or at Rama front were present at those briefings. So when it comes to that kind of communication, it was immediate in terms of superiors to subordinates as well." What you're referring to here would be the daily briefings you already referred to a few moments ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant the briefings convened by Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would suggest that the witness be provided with a copy of the text in Croatian, because both with this question and the previous question, the relevant element of the time-period is in question. So from the quotations, we can't gain an insight into what period of time is being referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, for reference purposes, this is contained -- and the statement, if we can provide it - I think the witness actually has it - is numbered as Exhibit 3D03712, and it's in the binder that Ms. Nozica has provided to the Chamber, the second binder from her.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I help? It's page 28/29 in the B/C/S, if I've got it right. But I would also like to suggest that the time of the briefing be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that help, to Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the place in the statement; it's page 28 and 29? I'd just like to return to what you say: "Anyway, during those briefings led by General Praljak ..." So is it correct that General Praljak also led certain briefings or conducted certain briefings for the commanders in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, General Praljak, and I'm speaking on the basis of my recollections, began to hold briefings after the January conflict, when I was able to communicate with the forward command post of the military district in Prozor, and the location was Dekorativa, which was a textile factory, the premises of a textile factory, and that's where the headquarters were put up. So that the answer to that is when I was able to leave Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje sometime after the 20th, those briefings were presided over by General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And were these daily briefings at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefings were with the unit commanders, and they were mostly a summary of the daily activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, until when did these briefings basically last that you're referring to? If you could just give the Court an idea of the time range.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These briefings started sometime on the 10th of January, 1993, and ended sometime in early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And those conducted by General Praljak, did they also go straight through to the period in early March?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Praljak joined these briefings after the 25th of January, and I don't know if it was him who chaired the briefings. For the most part or most often, it was done by Colonel Siljeg, the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But in your statement, you say: "Anyway, during those briefings led by General Praljak --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Kruger. A follow-up question, Witness. You said that you went to these briefings. I would like to know whether these briefings were headed by Siljeg and whether -- and Mr. Praljak was sitting aside, or whether the briefing was headed by Mr. Praljak and Siljeg was just attending, if you see the difference between the two situations. Could you tell me which one prevailed as to who headed these meetings, these briefings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was Colonel Siljeg who chaired the majority of the briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
