utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was General Praljak sitting; on his right or just anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he would be sitting next to some of the commanders on the right-hand side [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Colonel Siljeg was chairing the meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Colonel Siljeg conducted the briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. You are slightly changing your testimony. First you said you believe -- you believe that, which cannot be understood in any other way than you're not quite sure. Now you have been affirmative. Are you quite sure or you still believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure that Colonel Siljeg conducted the briefings, but quite simply General Praljak was in the room starting from after the 20th of January, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to the translation or the record. When Your Honour, on page 48, lines 20-21, is the answer -- when you asked the witness, he said: [In English] "Well, he would be sitting next to some of the commanders on the right-hand side." [Interpretation] The witness actually said: [In English] "He would be sitting next to some of the commanders or on the right-hand side," obviously referring to your question of Siljeg right side. But perhaps that would be cleared. And somehow that reflects also in that recent response of the Prosecutor on the additional question of Judge Trechsel, but maybe it should be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tokic, General Praljak's presence at those briefings, did he participate in those briefings, also impart information, give instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he did join in into the briefings, and I think he was a good motivator. And he also would come up with proposals, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And a good motivator, in the sense of inspiring you, as commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He quite simply encouraged us to gain strength and not to make unreasonable requests, and that we should approach our tasks as professional soldiers and responsible soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In your statement, I think it's the second statement that you made, in the English version it is page 34, and I think it is actually the last page of that statement, you're referring -- you were asked about General Praljak's style of communication, and I think that this refers to a meeting in October 1993, and you say: "Look --" do you have that question where you were asked about General Praljak's style of communication? Let me read to you: "Look, it's very hard to extract details from that meeting and say how General Praljak behaves in such conditions. The fact is General Praljak has a very specific way of communicating, he is sharp, curses a lot while he communicates. I don't think that meeting or communication was much different." Does this describe, to your mind, General Praljak's style of communication? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your information only, pages 8 to 9, this is 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, you're saying "3D," but what 3D?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D42-5351.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may perhaps help. I think the exhibit number referred to is 3D03712, and I think Ms. Pinter has given the page number, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I have only one more question at this stage regarding General Praljak's communication, and that refers to your statement. On page 18 of the English version, and I don't know if Ms. Pinter can help us to identify exactly where in the B/C/S version it is, but you're commenting on the 1st of August, 1993, where General Praljak issues a command for units to return to Uskoplje from the front-lines, and I'll just read to you very briefly: "On July 31, part of the HVO units retreated from Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje county, that is, from ...," and then certain locations are mentioned. "In the morning hours of August 1, all of these units were on the territory of Pidris. In that moment, General Praljak issued a command for units to return to Uskoplje front-lines." Now, my first question to you is: Do you recall receiving such an order from General Praljak which you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, General Praljak climbed the tank and said, Follow me to Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I think you've answered my second question. I wanted to ask: How was this order issued, written or verbally? But it seems that it was verbally and by example; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, orally and by example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, when General Praljak issued an order, they were obeyed? You had no qualms about obeying an order which came from General Praljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this took place on the 1st of August, 1993, and within all this mayhem and chaos, any commander with the rank of general would be obeyed who was willing to risk his own life. Any general who would climb a tank and, by example, call the army and the troops to follow him, that would be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you did not question his authority?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a commander, at a tactical level, never asks his superiors whether they have the appropriate authority for command and control. That's rule number 1. It is simply accepted as such on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So let's step on to another topic. I'd now like to explore with you the relations between you and Mr. Fahrudin Agic, and then perhaps also more broadly you -- or, sorry, the HVO and the Territorial Defence, or later the armija of the ABiH. Now, before starting on that, the Chamber has heard evidence already that a hot-line existed at UNPROFOR connecting the HVO and the ABiH units in Gornji Vakuf. Are you aware of that? Sir, I'm not referring to any document yet, so you needn't look in the binder yet.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, between myself and the commander of the 1317th [as interpreted] Brigade, Mr. Agic, was a wire connection, and we were able to talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this capability of talking to each other, did that serve to also diffuse situations during that period, tensions between the two sides, or did it contribute to it, at least?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have established this communication line in order to exchange information and inform each other about all the events taking place in the area of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. First, just look at something very general, and I'm referring to your statement once again. And in the English version, it's page 25 of your statement. I'll just read to you, and you needn't look at that. You can leave it. You were asked, in your statement, about whether it was difficult to maintain discipline, and I think this was with reference to the period surrounding October 1992, and your answer to this, what you responded was: "Yes, yes, because lower-ranking officers, to start with, they didn't want to run afoul of their neighbours with whom they lived just yesterday. They didn't want to take responsibility for construction of a system." Now, sir, is that correct, what you stated there, that in the ABiH units, comprised of local people from Gornji Vakuf, and in the HVO unit, comprised of locals from Gornji Vakuf, these people had previously been neighbours and friends?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you either don't have a proper translation here or you are trying to say something that I never said in my statement. My statement referred to my low-ranking officers who were in command of adjacent units in HVO and were unwilling to report them, so that higher-ranking officers would take disciplinary measures against them. And the rule book, disciplinary rule book, stipulates that the lowest-ranking officer that can impose disciplinary measures, such as detention or transfer, was company commander; therefore, I never mentioned anywhere my Bosniak neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now understand that. Let's move on to, then, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kruger. There is one element which makes me doubt about your answer, Witness. It's true that this passage does not speak of Muslims, but it speaks of neighbours, friends, "with whom they lived just yesterday." Now, if this were referring to their own men, the "yesterday" would not make sense, because they are still living, of course, with the men. They were supposed to report if they were undisciplined. Could you explain that, or is that a mistake of translation, the "yesterday"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm talking about discipline in my units, and my commanders of squad platoons and companies are requested to carry out their tasks. They're also requested to implement, both on their neighbours and their troops, the Rules of Service, and if they fail to do so, they should suffer consequences. And this is what my statement is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I fail to understand something. Why are they requested to implement Rules of Service on their neighbours? On their troops, yes, but why on their neighbours? That's what the translation says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind the time-frame that we are talking about, my units were engaged in implementing orders on the front-line facing the Army of Republika Srpska. Each time when I have to carry out the rotation or replacement of my troops, I issue an order which regulates the terms, saying that 48 hours prior to being sent out to carry out tasks, the troops, who are at the moment in civilian clothes and working the land, should be served a written summons to come and carry out the tasks. This is followed then by lining the men up, counting them, a medical examination to confirm whether they are fit or not fit for carrying out these tasks, checking the medical certificates, et cetera. Only the company commander is entitled to justify an absence of a soldier, but without, by doing so, diminishing the capability of the unit for carrying out the specific tasks. Everything else is simply subject to disciplinary measures. You either bring your troops for interview -- and in order to bring the soldier for interview, he has to be reported to the battalion commander who was being tasked with carrying out the rotation of troops, and in that context I'm talking about discipline in units. There were incidents in which a company commander or a platoon commander failed to report a soldier who never appeared because the soldier was his relative, a friend, or a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So what you are saying, if I understand you correctly, is that the Rules of Service apply also to persons who at a certain moment are at home, milking their cows, ploughing their fields, whatever, if they are susceptible to come back to service. The Rules of Service also apply to civilians who are not soldiers at the moment, but potential and previous soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me make it clear. A brigade has its mobilisation schedule, more than 300 [as interpreted] soldiers. We have no barracks where we can keep the soldiers in training and preparation. We have a front-line facing the Army of Republika Srpska for which, for one shift, we needed up to 350 troops. We are keeping a smaller number of troops on standby in the event of a sudden attack by the enemy on the front-line. Over 50 per cent of these soldiers were engaged in their regular daily work in the field or on the farm or in a private business. That is why they are called up 48 hours in advance, so that it would give them ample time to receive information about the impending task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tokic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe just a transcript correction. Page 56, line 6, the witness said, if I'm not wrong - this is what I heard - 1.300 soldiers, total number of members in the brigade, and the transcript reflects only 300. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tokic, just before stepping off this idea, the notion, however, of neighbours and friends having an impact on the relationship between the two conflicting parties or the atmosphere in Gornji Vakuf, I'd just like to ask you, the fact -- it is a fact that Muslims and Croats had been living harmoniously in Gornji Vakuf for some time prior to 1992 and 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fact, and that still is a fact up to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And that being a fact, it means that probably many Muslims had Croat friends and many Croats had Muslim friends prior to that, to 1992 and 1993, and they even have these friends until now, and neighbours, for that matter; isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So when a conflict broke out in Novi Travnik and in Prozor at a later stage, isn't it also safe to say, then, that the local Croats and the local Muslims in Gornji Vakuf, they weren't very keen on fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were in constant communication when we were talking about this region, and we were talking to each other all the time. I also had a number of Muslims in my unit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at a document which we've already looked at previously during your evidence. And if you go to the Prosecution document binder, it's Exhibit P00778. You'll see tabs along the side of the binder, and if you go to P000778, the second document, you'll see that it starts with the English version, but you can look at the original language version which will appeared second. Now, sir, this is your letter to the Gornji Vakuf Territorial Defence, and it's the letter concerning the gruesome murder of citizen Salih Grizic. That's the case or the incident where a soldier, Vlatko Rajic, had beheaded a Muslim, and this is of the 19th of November, 1992. Now, what I'd like to refer you to is the -- in your first paragraph -- well, it's only the second paragraph, then, and a few lines down, you say: "We sincerely sympathise with the relatives, acquaintances and friends of the late Salih Grizic." And further down you say: "We address all Muslims and members of the Territorial Defence in Gornji Vakuf municipality, hoping and wishing that this murder will not be used to further widen the gap that appeared between Croatian and Muslim people in the territory of Gornji Vakuf. Those who are trying to use this murder as a political means with the purpose of stirring up hatred between Croats and Muslims are not doing a favour to Croats or Muslims." Now, my first question to you is: When you wrote these words and sent this letter, were you absolutely sincere in your hope that the conflict between Croats and Muslims, that that gap would not further widen? And we're speaking about the gap between Croat and Muslim people in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I wrote this letter at the time this happened, and in my letter I express my feelings and sentiments, emotions, and my wishes to prevent the situation from becoming politicised, and I went on, on internal television, together with Mr. Agic, with this information, and we wanted to clarify this by means of direct communication. So, quite simply, my intentions were sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what you do express here, that would be pretty representative of the view generally held by the local Croats and the local Muslims residing in Gornji Vakuf; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, only somebody who does not wish goodwill to himself would be happy to see a conflict break out. We all wanted to prevent a conflict, and that was true of every soldier, every inhabitant of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, we'll look in a few moments about who the people were who were then fostering the conflict or fanning the flames, but you mentioned that you and Mr. Agic, that you then went on the local TV to appeal to the people to calm down, the people of Gornji Vakuf. Now, we had the evidence before the Court of Colour Sergeant Andrew Williams who was the information officer with the Cheshire Regiment. That was BritBat. Did you know or do you recall Mr. Williams, Andrew Williams?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major James, and with all due respect to the person, I don't remember him and the captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to read you a short excerpt from his testimony, and this is an excerpt he testified on the 6th --

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What document number is that? I don't seem to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This won't be a document. This was just evidence that has been presented in court. Just for the record, it's the transcript of the 16th of October, 2006, and it's transcript page 8448 from lines 3 to 10. The witness said: "Initially, during the early part --" he's referring to October and then later January. "Initially, during the early part of our tour, a tour such as this particular -- such as this particular moment in time, the local commanders used to sort it out between themselves with the assistance of Major Roux. They were -- both of the local commanders knew each other and tried -- whenever their soldiers were starting to become a problem, they did actually try to stop it. Very rarely did they have to at this stage, did they ever ask a higher level or were constrained by a higher level in what --" and this is an error in the transcript, "in what they did or said." Now, sir, this essentially confirms that you and your counterpart were often involved in diffusing potential conflict between the two sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Agic and I had to intervene very frequently. I would go into the field and he would mostly stay in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did the two of you trust each other?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that we trusted each other, but we cooperated mutually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, if we can move on to an exhibit in the Prosecution binder, Exhibit 1D00947. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly. It's 1D00947. It's in the last third of your binder. Now, sir, this is a report of the 6th of November by Mr. Ivan Saric on events in Gornji Vakuf from the 19th to the 31st of October, 1992. And the first question: Did you know Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivan Saric was the president of the Croatian Defence Council in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph, in the middle of that paragraph, it says: "On Monday, 19 October 1992, a member of Gornji Vakuf HVO had a conversation with the commander of BiH Army and the president of SDA for Gornji Vakuf, when it was concluded that the events in Novi Travnik must not and would not spread ... and that the situation would be manageable." The report then goes on to describe some tensions in Gornji Vakuf, and with well-armed HVO and ABiH soldiers present in every part of town, and then it says that Mr. Agic ascribes the tension to the movement of an HVO unit through Gornji Vakuf from Prozor to Novi Travnik. On page 2 in the English, it then says: "In agreement with the commander of the HVO Gornji Vakuf armed forces, they convened a meeting of all responsible people in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf." And then this bit: "The mere announcement of the meeting in a composition like this, and the knowledge thereof, gave hope to many, restored peace and even prevented possible conflict on that day." So, sir, from this -- well, first of all, the commanders being referred to of the HVO Gornji Vakuf, that would be you?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wouldn't be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that the commander convened it, but the president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My question, however, it doesn't matter whether you were present at that meeting or not, but it concerns this part: "The mere announcement of the meeting in a composition like this and the knowledge thereof gave hope to many." Would you agree that this confirms what we've been talking about earlier, that the locals in Gornji Vakuf, they weren't out for a fight, they didn't want to fight each other, they wanted peace in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can't give you a yes-or-no answer. We know from before that Mr. Saric and Mr. Abdulah Topcic, for all intents and purposes, did not communicate well and that, quite simply, they were obstructing command and control of the commanders of units, especially when it came to the BH Army. Mr. Agic, for instance, always made a pretext and said that the Patriotic League units, which already on the 10th of May, 1992, had taken control of the hotel, were not under his supervision, nor were the Green Berets who were commanded by Hanefija Prijic. So the question now arises as to who was in command of these units, so that if you looked at the document, you'll probably have seen that Mr. Topcic did not actually want to attend that meeting because Mr. Saric had convened it, and he didn't recognise Mr. Saric or the HVO, so he didn't want to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's correct. We'll be looking at the -- or exploring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, early this morning I asked you what the relationship was between the army and the political authorities, and you answered by saying the army was doing its job and the political authorities were doing other things, and now you're saying exactly the opposite. So I have a hard time reconciling this. Either you did not understand my question correctly, which is a possibility, of course, but now you're telling us that Mr. Saric interfered in the control and command of the army, which is exactly what I was trying to elicit this morning. But this morning, you said, No, but now you're saying, Yes. I'm having a hard time with your answers. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, may I provide an explanation? You asked me about the relationship between the commander of the HVO and a BH Army commander. You didn't ask me about communications between the political structures, between Mr. Topcic and Mr. Saric, for instance. The communication between me and Commander Agic was good. However, their communication was not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you had not understood my question. My question dealt with the relationship between you, as commander of the HVO, so a military man, and Mr. Ceric, president of the municipality. This is what I wanted to know about this morning, and you answered by saying, I was do what I had to do. And I drew the conclusion that there was no interference whatsoever, and now it seems that there were, so I'm trying to understand. I'm just noting this down. I'm not drawing any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would appreciate a direct answer to that question, because I understand Mr. Saric at one point was -- not only was he deposed, but also he was put on the front-line by the HVO, which clearly shows that if he was any person of authority, certainly he would not be on the front-line, dodging bullets. So I would appreciate an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Saric had no authority in terms of control and command, command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's look, in the same document, page 2, the third paragraph, also in your version the third paragraph, I think. And here it reports that: "According to the commander of the army, Fahrudin Agic, he had issued an order for his units to be in a state of readiness and to take the previously-determined points in and around the town because of the passage of the HVO unit going from Prozor towards Novi Travnik. On the other side, Zrinko Tokic, the staff commander, in his own words, had to respond to that with similar moves in order to prevent possible unpleasant surprises. In that way, the units found themselves in a stalemate situation, the situation of tension and anticipation, which could be turned into a destructive avalanche by anyone or anything." Now, sir, doesn't this actually sum up quite nicely the situation in Gornji Vakuf, that there's no real reason for conflict, but the ABiH feels threatened and then they take certain measures, defensive posturing measures, and then you, on the HVO side, have to respond thereto, or thought you had to respond thereto?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, feelings are subjective, but according to military principles, 3.000 members of the BH Army and 1.700 members [as interpreted] of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, do they have the same force, and which side should be concerned and fearful of their position?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I think we should correct the transcript on page 65, line 5. It says that the HVO had 1.700 members or, rather, soldiers. Can the witness put that right? I think it would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. 1.700 HVO members.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: [B/C/S spoken], "1.700" [realtime transcript read in error "2.700"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in short, the sides were watching each other very closely, and each side thought it had to respond the other side's actions, in short, without judging the right or wrong of it at this stage? Okay, I see you're kind of shaking your head. You agree with that -- or you don't disagree, at least, with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that both sides, quite simply, were on the alert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On page 3 of the English -- I'm sorry, page 2 of the English version, right at the bottom -- sorry, my mistake. Page 3 of the English version, and it would be probably the fifth or the sixth-to-last paragraph in the B/C/S version, just briefly, it says: "Owing to the HVO staff commander and probably the ABiH staff commander for Gornji Vakuf, the conflict did not spread to the surrounding villages, except for ..." So once again you and Mr. Agic, you solved the problem or diffused the tension; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I did have direct communication with Mr. Agic over the wire, but when we had to go out into the field, I was in the field, myself, to all intents and purposes, and Mr. Agic would send a battalion commander or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for stepping in, but after Ms. Tomanovic intervened and raised the question of the record and "1.700," now we have a worse situation according to which the witness confirmed that the number was 1.700 HVO members, and afterwards the interpreter's note was -- the record says "2.700." I think that's a mistake in the transcript. Which figure did the witness say, and what did the interpreter say, and were they all his soldiers or not? Because now we have a confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can. The Ante Starcevic Brigade numbered approximately 1.300, [B/C/S spoken]. The home guards had about 270. The MUP members of the military police and military conscripts who were in the Bruno Busic Brigade, now, when you add all that up, you should get 1.700, [B/C/S spoken]. They were domicile members from Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, remaining with this document, you've already referred to Mr. Topcic, Mr. Abdulah Topcic, who was the president of the SDA, and at the end of this report excerpts from Mr. Topcic's speech are reported, and this is the fourth-last paragraph of the document and, it says here, are examples from his speech. And then quotation marks: "What the gentleman and that imbecile Boban have in mind will not come true. We do not recognise the Croatian Defence Council. We won't be part of the HZ-HB," or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. "We won't be Croats with Muslim religion. We will get prepared and we will fight against HZ-HB until the last man." Now, on this -- oh, sorry, let me just go a little bit further: "We note that other representatives of the Muslim people did not affirm his words, but they did not condemn him either." Now, on this I'd like to ask you: The Court has heard evidence, so you don't disagree, that Gornji Vakuf was being claimed as part of the HZ-HB or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; the intention was to include it in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you knew it at that stage as well? We're talking about October 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew in October 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So if we look at what Mr. Topcic is saying, basically, it was also known in October 1992 that at least some of the Muslims were not pleased with the idea of including Gornji Vakuf within the HZ-HB. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that most of the Muslims saw the organisation for Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And it's also correct that the Muslims were actually in the majority in Gornji Vakuf, so it was unlikely that the aim could be achieved of including Gornji Vakuf in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1991 population census showed that 56 per cent were Bosniaks and 43 per cent were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with the notion that to include Gornji Vakuf within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, given its reluctant Muslim majority, that it wasn't going to happen, it wouldn't be possible? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me, as a commander, to make political assessments as to what is possible and what is not possible. There were two different conceptions, places and positions, Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and each side, in the political sense, advocated its own concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay, we'll come back to that point at a later stage. I think the next document I'm leaving. Sir, just very briefly, if you could look at document -- I had a few other documents in here which also tracks the cooperation or the efforts by you and Mr. Agic to diffuse situations, but have a look for a moment at 3D00508. This is a joint order by Mr. Siljeg, and signature -- the other signature is illegible. It's dated the 30th of January. Do you have it? You're looking at the wrong document. 3D --

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you tell me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 3D00508. Right, now you have it. The 30th of January, a joint order from Mr. Siljeg, and then the other signature is illegible. Would you know who the other signee is, the one on the right-hand side? Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as chance would have it, I do know who the person who signed there is. I think it's Mr. Emir Bijedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is to the HVO Gornji Vakuf Command and the BH Army Gornji Vakuf Command, and it says: "Pursuant to the existing situation in the area of Gornji Vakuf municipality, after the combat actions, in order to avert consequences and normalise life of citizens, we order to both HVO and BH Army: "To form joint expert teams to restore ..." Point 1, electricity; number 2, water; number 3 would be garbage cartage, et cetera. Number 5: "As responsible men for the realisation, I appoint Fahrudin Agic and Zrinko Tokic." At that stage, were you and Mr. Agic serious and sincere in your intention to perform this order?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that we were serious, but we did, indeed, carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. Now, sir, if we could go to Exhibit 4D00421. It's further on from where you are now, about three documents further on. 4D00043 -- sorry, it's -- no, the next. It's 4D00421. It's the third-last document in your binder. Now, this is an order from Mr. Arif Pasalic on the 14th of January, and it's an ABiH order which goes to the 1st Mostar Brigade and then a few other ABiH addressees as well. And just to confirm, you were aware that Mr. Pasalic was the counterpart of General Petkovic at this stage in January?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minor objection. I think that my learned colleague made a small mistake. I don't think that they were at the same line of command. Pasalic was counterpart of Mr. Siljeg, just in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I won't pursue this point in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is this order of Mr. Pasalic, and it says -- and if we go to the second paragraph: "Establish close cooperation with HVO brigade commands in the joint planning, carrying out of large-scale combat activities, especially along the axis of ...," and then it gives certain locations. Point 3: "Avoid conflicts with the HVO at any cost, regardless of the attempts of extremist factions, doing everything to ensure that the relations between Muslims and Croats deteriorate." Now, sir, my question to you is: Based on this order of the 14th of January, would you agree that is an indication that the ABiH was actually trying to be reasonable in Gornji Vakuf? This isn't an aggressive posture being taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I believe that my question, which I would like to ask from the witness, is about the same thing which you tried to ask him about, and it is about point 1 of the order. And I would like to ask the witness if the reference to enemy territory in the first line, of what does it mean, in his view? And let me quote the first point: "Intensify sabotage activities deeper inside enemy territory, at the KM/command post, at the artillery's VP/firing positions, in rear services," et cetera. Do I take it that the "enemy territory" in this case would have meant actually Serbian or Republika Srpska territory? Because otherwise the rest of the paragraphs are not very convincing, because actually from the second paragraph there is an important -- "appear for close cooperation with the HVO brigade," et cetera, et cetera. So what is your view about the "enemy territory" question? In your view, to which territory does it refer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to note that this, Arif Pasalic's order, commander of the 4th Corps, does not refer in any way to Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality and the ABiH units because these were directly commanded by the 3rd Corps with headquarters in Zenica. If you allow me to respond to your question, then I believe that under item 1, reference is being made to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is what I also felt. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just clarify. The 4th Corps, which Mr. Pasalic is referring to, what was their area of responsibility? It's just that I don't mislead you here.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended with Prozor municipality, due north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So when there is talk about "establish close cooperation with HVO brigade commands in the joint planning," this "HVO brigade commands," would that include your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was North-Eastern Herzegovina Operations Zone -- I apologise, South-Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's not -- and then -- waste further time on this document. I'd like to return to the -- to the flag incidents which we've heard about over the Christmas period. Now, you mentioned or you also testified yesterday that a HOS flag was hoisted on a pole or a post, but I'd just like to explore with you whether there weren't more flag incidents and that we don't get them all mixed up. First of all, if I can refer to your statement on page 7, and that's your first statement. And then just for the record, that's Exhibit 3D03712, and the B/C/S version should appear on your screen, hopefully. But I'd like to read to you. You state: "And this relates to Christmas 1992 in villages of Voljice, Drazev, Duradbegovic Dolac, Ivica, and Planinica," and you say that these villages were 90 per cent Muslim. And then I'll quote: "Catholic Croats, according to their tradition, decorate their towns, and there was some problems regarding the decorating of the towns and showing Croatian flags or flags of the Croat people." Now, you don't disagree with this, because you already testified to this, about the custom of decorating and why flags were used. However, what I'd like to ask you, and it bodes on what Mr. Karnavas asked you, whether this was a provocation, these villages which you are referring to, you say were 90 per cent Muslim, so a very small number of Croats, raising -- oh, and at this stage, if we can add, it seems that the situation or the relationships were very sensitive in Gornji Vakuf between the various groups. There was a lot of tension. Now, sir, under those circumstances, isn't the mere fact of raising a Croat flag more than only a Christmas celebration; doesn't it have also a political signal?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when we talk about this portion that you have quoted, this refers to the defence line facing the Army of Republika Srpska, where my units were in the process of carrying out their tasks. Passing through these villages and defending these villages populated by Muslims, or 90 per cent populated by Muslims, when it comes to decorating the town for Christmas, this is an ancient tradition of the Croatian people elsewhere, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we used to do that back in 1990, 1991, et cetera, and nobody was bothered by that. Only in 1992 did -- a few people came forward and said that they had a problem with that. In a document, it is stated that the MUP or, rather, the police of the army have found three flags and they put them back. So we were cooperating with the army on this particular issue. Obviously, they didn't mind seeing the flags hoisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, we shall have the break now because it's time for the break, and the break will last 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Kruger, you've had one hour so far. You've been granted two hours. If you make an effort and try and be efficient in your time management, and if there is not much redirect, we will be able to finish today, which would mean that the witness could go back home today. This is what I have to tell you, Mr. Kruger. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before we lose this page from our screens, I'm talking about page 73, the sentence in line 20. The witness said, as it reads here: [In English] "In the document, it is stated that the MUP, or, rather, the police of the army have found ..." [Interpretation] The witness said "the military police" rather than "the police of the army." That can have multiple meanings. And the last sentence in line 23, the witness said, as it is recorded: [In English] "Obviously, they didn't mind seeing the flags hoisted." [Interpretation] But after that, he added "but the other's minded." The others thought that it was not a small matter; that the army, obviously they didn't mind seeing the flags hoisted, but others did. [Interpretation] And I can take this opportunity to draw the witness's attention to something that the interpreters told us during the break, is that you be careful when you use the terms "vojska" and "armija." We understand that when you say "armija" this normally refers to the ABiH, but when we say "vojska," any army would mean that, and we would specify which particular army you had in mind, and this is actually the root of this mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tokic, just before the break we were talking about the flag incident, and you mentioned - it was also previously in your evidence, it's also in your statement - about a flag that was taken -- or three flags that were taken down, and then they were returned. They were returned by your MPs and put back in -- or they were returned by the TO, and these flags were then put in place again. And I think they were thereafter taken down again, but not returned. Do you recall that evidence? That's basically correct, or my paraphrasing of it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said that they had first been taken down, then returned, then taken down again. And after that, we had no feedback information as to what happened with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, this incident, if I'm not mistaken, was on the 23rd and 24th of December, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These incidents took place between the 24th and 27th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Would you -- you wouldn't disagree that the fact that the Territorial Defence or the TO returned those flags the first time they were taken down, that was a very conciliatory gesture on their part?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the TO or, rather, the ABiH looked benevolently at the Croatian flags, but there were other extremists who didn't see this issue in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the fact that these flags were being taken down, and the fact that the flag had now been returned, it must have been clear to Croats in Gornji Vakuf that the whole issue of a flag -- putting up a flag is sensitive. So under those circumstances, do you still stick with your story that it was not a provocation to put those flags up again?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just before moving on, in the bit of your statement that I quoted to you, you mentioned that it was decorating of the town and showing Croatian flags or flags of the Croat people. Could you tell us, what are -- what's the difference between this? What is a Croatian flag?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia is a tricolour, red, white and blue, with the Croatian coat of arms, without the crown, if I may call it the crown on the flag, which symbolises the counties and the regions in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But what, then, would the second category be, flags of the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a flag, in red, white and blue, with the ancient historical Croatian coat of arms in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Would this be the flag of the Republic of Croatia or not? Is that a different flag?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, having spoken about that flag incident, there was a flag incident on the 4th of January, 1993, which resulted in a Muslim shooting at or over the flag and then, in turn, being shot, himself. And there was testimony before this Court on that once again from Andrew Williams from the Cheshire Regiment, and he testified about the events, and he said: "Afterwards, on diffusing the situation," and this is his transcript on the 16th of October, 2006, transcript page 8447 from line 8 onwards, the question is: "And what was Mr. Tokic's reaction to this incident, because I presume you sat around a table again with the local commanders to diffuse the situation?" And the answer of Mr. Williams was: "Again, there was a meeting with the two local commanders and Major Roux, and again they managed to stop the situation spiraling out of control." Now, he put you -- according to his evidence, you were knowledgeable of this incident, but now I'd just like to take you a little bit earlier in his evidence, when he's talking about the situation, and his testimony is that this flag was being raised at a school in Gornji Vakuf which was being used as an HVO barracks, and he testified that a Croatian television crew had come to film the event, and on that he eventually said: "You would not expect a TV crew from a foreign country to come and watch the raising of a flag outside a school." Now, sir, my question is: Is it correct that on the 4th of January, there was a flag-raising at a school being used as an HVO barracks which resulted in the shooting incident mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my statement and testimony, I precisely describe both the flag and the place where it happened. That was a HOS flag, the flag of the Croatian Armed Forces which is a small unit which operated in the area of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality and had the strength of a platoon. This particular flag was hoisted up on a lighting pole -- a street lighting pole if front of Radusa Hotel. When members of the Bosniak ethnic community tried to pull the flag down, one soldier or more soldiers - I'm not sure - fired shots above the heads of these soldiers, which made them flee in all directions. So what you mentioned about the elementary school and the incident, itself, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, let's move to another document, P01653.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My dear colleague, I'm awfully sorry, but maybe that could cause a problem. It is the question of the transcript. Page 77, line 24, the witness said: "That was a HOS flag, the flag of," as it is written in the transcript "the Croatian armed forces." I don't believe that the witness said such a thing. I didn't get it in original language, but that simply can be -- I think that he said "Croatian forces." But, anyway, whatever, I think that should be clarified, because this could mean many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard that. Could you clarify what your reference was?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HOS was simply a small unit of some 30-odd troops that was formed in the area of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality. It was attached to the 113th Battalion. I was not in command of that unit, and that was the banner of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when other units caused problems, were you also called upon to solve those problems with Mr. Agic -- yes, Mr. Agic, or were the commanders of those units actually then called upon to solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, we endeavoured to resolve this through direct contacts with Mr. Agic. Sometimes we would call the commanders of those concrete units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, this HOS unit of about 30 men, platoon strength, they were subordinated or part of the HVO, in essence?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not part of my brigade. They had their own battalion that was commanding them directly from Tomislavgrad, and I have no information about whether they were incorporated into the HVO or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn to the document that I was referring to, P01653. You have the document roughly in the middle of your binder, 1653. Now, sir, this document is a report by you, dated the 11th of March, 1993. It seems you have it now. It's a report by you, 11th of March, 1993, and it reports on events in Gornji Vakuf between 18 June 1992 and 13 January 1993. In the last paragraph, in the middle, there we see you're reporting on exactly the flag incidents in December 1992, but what I'd like to refer you to is in the second paragraph, towards the end of the second paragraph, after the reference to Mr. Abdulah Topcic and the criminal Salih Cajdin. It says: "On 11 July 1992, four members of the Garavi Sabotage Unit came from Bugojno to Gornji Vakuf to the coffee bar in Odvudac [phoen] and a fight broke out with guests of Muslim ethnicity." Now, sir, my question to you is: The Garavi unit, what unit was this?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the unit with that name was active within the brigade called "Elgin Kvaternik" from Bugojno, and it was -- it specialised in sabotage, diversionary, and reconnaissance work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And to which army did this unit originally belong?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the Croatian Defence Council unit, the Dr. Elgin Kvaternik Brigade, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This Garavi unit, is it correct that they continued -- or they continued to have a presence in Gornji Vakuf into 1993 as well?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived -- or most of them lived on the territory of the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality in the various settlements around Plavic [phoen] Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also correct that -- well, you've already mentioned about another unit from Tomislavgrad which was also present on the territory, but what other HVO units were present on the territory of Gornji Vakuf, apart from the Ante Starcevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, apart from the Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, there was also the -- well, a battalion -- well, it was called a battalion, but it had up to 60 men, from the Bruno Busic Regiment, and then the military police, and then there was a platoon-size unit from HOS, the brigade police, which was under my composition. They were units which had a mobilisation establishment and schedule and was made up of men from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. The presence of units and men not from the area of Gornji Vakuf, did that raise or cause tensions or increase -- let's say contribute to the tensions in the municipality between Muslim and Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the presence of the 305th Brigade of the BH Army, and later on part of the HVO units from the Tomislavgrad Military District, could significantly, well, raise tensions and lead to incidents in town, and the population could look upon this with anxiety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. And what about HVO units or elements of the HVO coming from Tomislavgrad, for instance; would that also raise tensions amongst Muslims or concerns amongst Muslims, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And as we've seen from this document, the members of the Garavi unit, they also caused problems?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, a lot of what we've talked about was focused on the local Muslims, the local Croats, in Gornji Vakuf actually wanting to avoid conflict, but the conflict was not avoided. Yesterday, you told us -- apologies. Yesterday, you told us, inter alia, that Serbs also provoked and -- or utilised the tensions to promote conflict, it seems that outside units promoted conflict, and then we have some extremists taking down flags, which also raises the tension. But let's look at some other factors which could also contribute to the raising of the tensions. And now I'd like to refer you to Exhibit P01184. It's earlier in your binder. Do you have the document? It's about the tenth document in, 1184. Do you have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to perhaps assist the witness in finding the document, please. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a letter by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and it is from -- if you look at the stamp, there's a date of the 18th of January, so it's around about the 18th of January, 1993. It's titled "Gornji Vakuf," and it's addressed to the Croatian Defence Council of the municipality and to the Croatian population of the Gornji Vakuf municipality. And the second paragraph reads: "From the report of the Defence Section of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, then from the contacts with your officials and officers, as well as on the basis of reports of objective media, it's obvious that the Muslim forces are intending to take over the rule, to enable HVO defensive activities --" or "disable --" sorry, or "to enable HVO defensive activities, and then, by applying terror, to cause an exodus of the Croat people from that area." Now, sir, in the light of what we've been talking about, what you've testified yesterday and today about attempts to calm the situation, avoid tension, cooperate -- the both sides are to cooperate with each other, wouldn't you agree that this, stating it's obvious that the Muslim forces are intending to take over the rule, it's not obvious at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the concentration of forces and the balance of forces speaks of intentions, and as a commander it is my duty to assess the forces being concentrated around the area of Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje. And for those reasons, the presence of the 305th Brigade from Jajce is an obvious attempt to change the balance of forces in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality. And as a soldier, I have to express my concern and ask my colleague, Mr. Agic, to have those forces sent back to where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. That may be so, but isn't it true that there wasn't an intention to take over the whole of Gornji Vakuf? This was all about the access routes to Central Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, there are no barracks, there were no barracks, and if they wanted to use the barracks, then they would have used the one in Travnik. So here, obviously, the intention was to deploy the units in such a way as to place Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Looking at the statement, where it says that the -- referring to the ABiH, that what they want to do is, by applying terror, to cause an exodus of the Croat people from that area, isn't it obvious to you that this is an over-statement? There wasn't an intention to chase Croats from this area, not amongst the local people?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I testified here and said that members of the Green Berets, in October 1992, maltreated Croats in the buildings they lived in or in an area which was 90 per cent Bosniak, and they all fled to the Croatian part of town after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I put it to you that in view of the fact that the local Muslims, the local Croats, in Gornji Vakuf, that as you've admitted, they were not keen on a conflict, they simply wanted peace and to coexist, I put it to you that what Dr. Prlic is writing here is aimed at stoking up the tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this point, Your Honour. It's not Dr. Prlic who's writing, even though he signed the document. It's rather unclear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I don't know what you were going to say, but the Prosecutor is putting a question to the witness, using a document that was written by your client, so let the witness answer, and then you'll -- because you are intervening, you're taking the floor in the midst of the question, and you're exerting pressure on the witness, and any reasonable trier of fact will immediately notice that you are interfering. The Prosecutor is just asking a question, so let the witness answer, and then you can say the Prosecutor did not put the question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I will allow the question, and then I will show that you are incorrect in your admonishment, because I'm trying to correct something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not admonish -- I didn't admonish you. I just said that the Prosecutor is putting a question and we want to have the answer from the witness, and then you can take the floor and say that the Prosecutor instrumented the question or what not, but later. Witness, before Mr. Karnavas takes the floor, how did you want to answer the Prosecutor's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor repeat his question, please, because I'm not quite sure of the specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, the question is that: You've said today -- you've admitted that essentially the local Croats, the local Muslims, in Gornji Vakuf didn't want a conflict; they wanted to -- they wanted peace. Now, I'm putting it to you, in that context, seeing a letter like this in the name of Dr. Jadranko Prlic, which mentions Muslims wanting to take over the rule in Gornji Vakuf and to apply terror to cause an exodus of Croatian people, I put it to you that this is actually stoking the tensions.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think that this goes in support of the Croatian population; that is, that they should stay and live in their homes and that they stay up there, in spite of the terror, and that the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna guarantees their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking a little bit further -- well, the next line, next paragraph, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Karnavas, do you want to take the floor? You have the floor, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The only point I wanted to make, Mr. President, is as follows: The implication is that this is a letter from Dr. Prlic, and clearly that is a misstatement and a mis-characterisation of the document. If you look very closely, it's from the HVO HZ-HB. The fact that Dr. Prlic is the one that signs it, it's not his letter. And so I understand the need to attribute power and authority to Dr. Prlic alone, but this is a communication that is being made on the basis of a meeting that was held by the HVO HZ-HB. There is a big difference. I understand I'm dealing with professional judges, but be that as it may, I do feel the need to bring that to the Court's attention and to make my record. That's all. I don't want to suggest anything else from that. The witness is clear -- can answer whatever other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, reading the second paragraph of this letter, it says: "Giving support to resisting such intentions, the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is determined to provide you with any form of help, including the force and combat readiness of the armed forces of the HVO." Now, sir, at that stage did you know what the HVO of HZ-HB was, the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you knew that Dr. Prlic was, as president, basically the most senior person or, shall I say, the -- to use a colloquial term, the prime minister of that body or the chair?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was president of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, whether he was prime minister or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Did you also know that Mr. Stojic was a member of that body?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Stojic was the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So this letter, did you see this letter at that stage in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you had seen this letter in January of 1993 and read this, would this have surprised you, would it have seemed out of the ordinary, or would you have accepted that, yes, this body does have the authority to make such a promise, that it will provide us with help, including the force and combat readiness of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think that when a commander receives a letter of this kind, the letter allays his concern for the fate of the territory which is under his charge and gives him hope that if the BH forces attack him, that he won't stand alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. But from what you're saying now, I gather that you would have had no doubt in your mind that the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, they possessed the necessary authority to back up a promise like this.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not in a position to judge whether they had the necessary authority to be able to put into practice things like this. It was sufficient for me to know that I wouldn't be alone if the BH Army were to attack Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So this would have assured you or reassured you. Sir, if I can quickly show or refer to a document which was shown yesterday and today, and it's document 3D00796, and I think it should be towards the end of your binder, about the seventh or the eighth document from the end. This is the document of 26 October 1993. And just for the record, it was also presented today under the number of 4D00803. Do you have the document, 3D --

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just take a moment, please? And may I have some assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've got the document. You remember we've spoken at length about this document. This is the one where various commanders of the HVO in your operational zone address an appeal to the government for -- to address and to look into certain problems to keep you going. What I'm interested in is the final page of the document, and it says, above the signees, it says: "Deliver to ..." You have that? "Deliver to the president of the HR-HB, the president of the HR-HB government, the minister of defence of the HR-HB, and the head of the General Staff of the HVO." Now, sir, this is 26 October 1993. Could I ask you, the fact that this letter is addressed to this group within the government, does that signify that you and the other signees viewed these people as the leadership with the authority to address your problems of the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we simply considered that these were competent individuals able to solve our problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was that based on your experience during the previous year, basically, the whole of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have such experience, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The president of the HR-HB, that would be Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is the first time that the commanders sat down and directly addressed the president and representatives of the authorities and government in the Community of Herceg-Bosna with respect to the problems listed in these items here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, our time is nearly finished, but just if we can try and finish on this specific point. The president of the HR-HB that you're addressing here, that's Mr. Boban, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The president of the HR-HB government, who was that? Is that Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, although at that point in time I didn't need to communicate. Later on, I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the minister of defence of the HR-HB, that's Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the head of the General Staff at that stage, was that Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak that you were addressing?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my recollections, it was Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Addressing the president of the HR-HB government, was that to him, in his personal capacity, judging from this?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We addressed him as president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, as direct person in command of the armed forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to conclude on this point, these were the people at that stage, and had been throughout the course of that year, who were responsible and, in the military chain of command, basically at the top?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operative sense, the chain of command does not go via the government and the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It would go via the head of the Main Staff, would it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via the Main Staff of the operative zones and the brigades, the independent battalions, and directly to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. But ultimately the question stands that: You, as one of these HVO commanders, you addressed this letter to these people because they were the people with the necessary authority to address your problems?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people controlled sufficient resources and had the possibility, in our opinion, of solving the problems, quite simply, which are listed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: There is something in transcript. This is line 18, page 89. The Prosecutor asked -- addressed him as -- addressing the president of HR-HB government, was it to him, in his personal capacity, judging from this, and the witness has answered meaning president of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, so I think that the witness didn't answer the question or said something which wasn't asked. It's not clear for me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the question or the comment. The reference to president of the HR-HB government in your response, when I asked you was this addressed to the president, personally, in his personal capacity, could you just repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as commander from the field, I came to attend the meeting. I signed this document. Now, as the distribution went, to whom, in what capacity, and all the rest of it, I simply don't have to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I -- sorry. [Interpretation] I'd just like to be of assistance to the Prosecutor. I think the witness is mixing up the functions. Perhaps the Prosecutor, when stating a function or position, could name a name, and then the witness would understand exactly what the Prosecutor was asking him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do we have time to complete that one now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue tomorrow, but we could also finish right away if the Defence has no redirect and if you're finished, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will have some questions in redirect, so we won't be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we will resume tomorrow. We'll adjourn, and we'll meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
